mains./projects/security-lab.html:
My projects

SENTINEL-X

My Raspberry Pi security lab. I’m getting Suricata logs into a dashboard and learning how to check the alerts.

← All projects

What I set up

I’m using a Raspberry Pi 5 and my Windows 11 laptop. Suricata runs on the Pi. I connect over SSH, and a Python/Flask app reads the event log and displays it in my browser.

The dashboard is working. I’m still editing the filtering and refresh code. This page shows the setup and the mistakes I ran into along the way.

I ran a Linux command in the wrong terminal

I tried to open the dashboard file with nano while I was still in Windows PowerShell. PowerShell returned “nano is not recognized.” I needed to connect to the Pi first, then edit the file there.

nano ~/sentinel-x-dashboard/app.py

That was a useful reminder to check the prompt before running a command. My Windows terminal and the shell on the Pi are different environments.

See the PowerShell error

Getting the app and browser connected

The Flask app runs on 127.0.0.1:5000 on the Pi. Opening localhost on my laptop does not reach that app by itself. I use an SSH tunnel from the laptop to forward the port.

I also checked whether anything was listening on port 5000 before starting the app:

sudo ss -lntp | grep ':5000'

ss lists sockets. The options show listening TCP ports and their processes; grep narrows the output to port 5000. I then started the app with the Python interpreter in its virtual environment.

~/sentinel-x-dashboard/venv/bin/python ~/sentinel-x-dashboard/app.py
See Flask running on the Pi

Checking that an alert really came through

I sent four pings to my router and checked Suricata’s alert log. The rule name was SENTINEL-X ICMP Test Alert. I then checked the same alert in the dashboard.

ping -c 4 192.168.1.1
sudo tail -n 10 /var/log/suricata/fast.log

-c 4 stops after four ping requests. tail -n 10 shows the last ten log lines. This was test traffic on my own network, not an attack.

The dashboard code I’m working on

The app reads /var/log/suricata/eve.json, separates alerts from flow events, and counts them. The table shows the time, source, destination and rule name. I added severity totals and started moving the browser updates to /api/events.

The browser fetches that endpoint before updating the counters:

const response = await fetch("/api/events");
See the code in the editor

Still working on

I need to finish checking the alert filters and automatic refresh after the latest edits, then try more rules and write down the results. Wazuh is a later step. For now, I’m focusing on understanding the Suricata logs and keeping the dashboard useful.

RAREST Fashion

A clothing website I’m building for a friend’s brand.

← All projects

What I worked on

I worked on the shop pages, product options, shopping bag and deployment. The site uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Cloudflare Workers and D1 behind the storefront.

mains./projects/helpdesk.html:
My projects

IT Help Desk Ticketing

A small Flask app for keeping track of support requests.

← All projects

The idea

I wanted to keep the ticket, assigned technician and troubleshooting history together. It connects to the kind of support work I’ve done with users, hardware and network problems.

How it works

The app uses Python, Flask and SQLite. Requesters see their own tickets, while technicians can work through the queue. A ticket change and its history entry are saved in the same database transaction.

What I checked

The saved test results include seven Flask test-client checks. The app uses parameterized SQL, CSRF checks and a session reset at login. It is still a local project with fictional tickets; browser testing and a production setup are further work.
mains./projects/sql.html:
My projects

SQL Business Analytics

SQL practice with generated retail orders.

← All projects

What I built

I used Python and SQLite to create sample orders, then wrote joins, CTEs and window functions to answer questions about revenue and customer groups. The data is generated, so there are no customer records here.

The join I had to be careful with

An order can have several line items. Joining those tables and summing the order total can count the same order more than once. The queries aggregate at order level first. I also used a left join to keep guest orders in the results.

How I checked the numbers

The saved dataset has 444 orders and 895 order lines. Five checks compare the totals, including whether customer segments reconcile to all orders. I store money in integer cents. The results are useful for checking the queries, not for claiming real business growth.

mains./projects/forecasting.html:
My projects

Retail Demand Intelligence

A Python forecasting exercise using generated retail data.

← All projects

What I compared

I compared a moving-average baseline with gradient boosting using pandas and scikit-learn. I kept later weeks separate for evaluation rather than randomly mixing the timeline.

What the results showed

In the saved holdout results, wMAPE was 26.8% for the baseline and 9.8% for gradient boosting. Those numbers describe this synthetic dataset. They don’t show savings for an actual store.

What I need to watch

The timing of each input matters. A model can look better if it gets information that would not have been available when a forecast was made. Weather availability is one limitation recorded in this project.

mains./case-studies/authentication.html:
Build notes

Login detection notes

A separate Python exercise with fictional login events.

← Build notes

What the rule looks for

The detector groups events by source, account and host. It checks for repeated failed logins followed by a success inside a five-minute window.

What I checked

The saved input produces two alerts, and the recorded test set has six checks. I use fictional records so I can change the sequence and see how the rule behaves.

What a match tells me

A matching pattern deserves a closer look. It could also come from someone mistyping a password or from shared devices. This exercise is separate from my Suricata setup; it is not a live SIEM feed.
mains./case-studies/sql-integrity.html:
Build notes

Checking my SQL totals

Notes from the retail SQL project.

← Build notes

The problem with order lines

Joining an order to its line items repeats the order fields on each matching row. If I sum the order total at that point, I can inflate revenue.

The approach in the queries

I aggregate at order level before grouping customers. A left join keeps guest orders, and integer cents keep monetary totals consistent.

How I checked it

The saved checks reconcile 444 orders and $59,578.20 in generated revenue. The segment counts add back to the order count. These checks tell me about the sample queries and data, not a real retailer.
mains./case-studies/deployment.html:
Build notes

Putting the portfolio online

Notes on moving from local files to my own domain.

← Build notes

Keeping the original

I kept the original Still Becoming site separate while developing the newer portfolio. That gave me a way to change the layout without overwriting the earlier work.

The site setup

Cloudflare Workers serves the pages and assets at ronnydonkor.com. Git tracks the source. The newer site has separate pages, shared CSS and JavaScript, and optimized images.

What needed checking

I checked routes, images and response handling. Search indexing also needed attention: robots settings, canonical URLs and the sitemap have to agree with the public domain. I’m continuing to improve the content as I add project evidence.

mains./pages/cloud.html:
Cloud / my work

Hosting my websites

What I’ve been doing with Cloudflare Workers, domains and deployment.

← Home

This portfolio

ronnydonkor.com runs through a Worker in my Cloudflare account. It serves the HTML pages, styles, scripts and images. I keep the site source in Git and make changes as I add to the portfolio.

RAREST Fashion

The clothing site uses Workers and D1. It involves more than serving static pages: the storefront needs product data and server-side checks. Checkout and messaging are separate parts of the setup, and the site is still under development.

Things I’ve worked through

I’ve worked on custom domains, redirects, routing and search-indexing settings. A deployed page still needs checking: whether links work, whether the right assets load, and whether search engines can access the public pages.

What’s next

I want to keep building my cloud knowledge alongside the security lab. AWS is my next area of study.
